name: Matruraivaradeeswarar Temple, Tiruppachilacchiramam
deity: Shiva as Matruraivaradeeswarar, with the goddess Balambigai (Balasoundari)
period: Ancient Shaiva shrine beside the Kollidam, sung in the Tevaram (7th century); medieval Chola-era temple with later additions
dynasty: Chola-era patrons (founding dynasty not firmly sourced)
summary: Matruraivaradeeswarar is the Tevaram shrine of Tiruppachilacchiramam, today's Thiruvasi, where tradition says Sambandar's hymn lifted a grievous illness from the daughter of the Kolli chieftain Kollimazhavan and where Sundarar's faith in the Lord's gold was tested.

sections.history: Thiruvasi lies on the northern bank of the Kollidam, a dozen kilometres or so from Tiruchirappalli, and was anciently called Pachilachiramam. It is one of the Paadal Petra Sthalams, praised in the Tevaram by both Sambandar and Sundarar of the seventh century, and the name of the modern town is understood as a softening of the old one. The temple is a Dravidian structure of the medieval Chola country, though some temple traditions hold the core shrine to be older still. In Sekkizhar's account of the saints, Sambandar came here after worshipping at Thirumanthurai. The Lord of the temple is called Matruraivaradeeswarar, a name explained in two ways: as the Lord who changed a saint's song from complaint to praise, and as the Lord who proved the true quality of gold, as a jeweller tests it on the touchstone.
sections.architecture: The temple faces east and is approached beneath two five-tiered towers. Within, the plan follows the classic sequence of sanctum, antarala, ardha mandapa and mukha mandapa, with the sanctum standing on a raised level in the central prakara. The Shiva linga is worshipped as Matruraivaradeeswarar, and the goddess Balambigai, also remembered as Balasoundari, has her own shrine. The shrine of Nataraja holds a rare and much-loved image, the Sarpa Nataraja, in which a snake lies beneath the Lord's lifted foot, in place of the dwarf figure Muyalagan, and his matted hair is tied in a knot. This form is bound up with the temple's best-known legend.
sections.legends: The great story of Thiruvasi is of a king's daughter. Kollimazhavan, the chieftain of the Kolli hills country, had a daughter stricken by a grievous seizure sickness, the illness the tradition calls muyalagan, and no physician could ease her. When he learned that the child-saint Sambandar was travelling this way after worshipping at Thirumanthurai, he brought her to the temple and laid her before the Lord. Sambandar sang the decad beginning Thunivalar Thingal, and as the hymn was sung the Lord took the sickness, turned it into a snake, and danced upon it, and the princess rose well. A second memory belongs to Sundarar. Needing gold to feed the poor, he asked the Lord and met silence, sang in vexation, and found gold along the path to the temple. Doubting it, he had it tested, and ashamed of his doubt he turned his song to praise. From this the Lord is known as the one who made the change and approved the gold.
sections.festivals: The principal festival is the eleven-day Brahmotsavam in the month of Vaikasi, in May or June. Tirukarthikai in November or December fills the temple with lamps, Arudra Darshan in Margazhi honours Shiva as the cosmic dancer, and Thai Poosam is kept in January or February. Maha Shivaratri and the monthly Pradosham are observed as at every Shiva temple. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Thiruvasi rewards a visit made with the story in mind. Enter beneath the eastern tower and come first to the sanctum of Matruraivaradeeswarar, then to the goddess Balambigai in her own shrine. Spend a few quiet minutes before the Sarpa Nataraja, whose snake and knotted hair bring the legend of the healed princess close. Families who pray for the health of an ailing child hold this place especially dear, and devotees of Sundarar recall the gold that tested a saint's trust. The town lies off the city's bustle by the Kollidam, and within the walls the temple keeps a calm that is easy to feel.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning and again from late afternoon into the evening, with a midday break; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left outside the temple.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Thiruvasi is on the northern bank of the Kollidam in Tiruchirappalli district, about 12 to 14 km from Tiruchirappalli city and its Chatram bus stand. Tiruchirappalli Junction is the main railway station, and Tiruchirappalli has the nearest airport. Buses, taxis and auto-rickshaws serve the town from the city, and the temple is easily found in the village.
